One-sentence verdict: Compliance Managers are not a "rule-checking administrative role"; they plan, direct or coordinate an organization's activities to ensure compliance with ethical or regulatory standards; O*NET defines the occupation as "plan, direct, or coordinate an organization's activities to ensure compliance with ethical or regulatory standards," and its tasks rank "report violations of compliance or regulatory standards to duly authorized enforcement agencies as appropriate or required" and "identify compliance issues that require follow-up or investigation" as the top two; this page follows the exact occupational scope of O*NET-SOC 11-9199.02.

The work of Compliance Managers can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is compliance programs and policy and training: develop or direct the development or implementation of compliance-related policies and procedures in the organization; verify that all regulatory policies and procedures have been documented, implemented and communicated; distribute written policies and procedures related to compliance activities; provide training to employees on compliance-related topics, policies or procedures; hold discussions on emerging compliance issues to ensure that management and employees understand the compliance reporting system and policies and practices; design or implement improvements in communicating, monitoring or enforcing compliance standards; and advise internal management or business partners on the implementation or operation of compliance programs. The second is monitoring, review and internal investigation: identify compliance issues that require follow-up or investigation; conduct or direct internal investigations of compliance issues; conduct periodic internal reviews or audits to ensure that compliance procedures are followed; monitor the compliance system to ensure it is effective; provide assistance to internal or external auditors in compliance reviews; collaborate with human resources to ensure a consistent disciplinary approach where compliance standards are violated; verify that software technology is in place to provide adequate oversight and monitoring in the required areas; and oversee internal reporting systems such as corporate compliance hotlines. The third is reporting, consulting and specialized compliance: report violations of compliance or regulatory standards to duly authorized enforcement agencies as necessary or required; file appropriate compliance reports with regulatory agencies; maintain documentation of compliance activities such as complaints received or investigation outcomes; consult with corporate attorneys as needed on difficult legal compliance issues; serve as a confidential point of contact for employees and management to communicate, seek clarification on difficult issues or report violations; prepare compliance operations and progress reports for management; keep up to date on industry changes, trends or best practices; develop risk management strategies based on assessments of product, compliance or operational risk; review promotional materials such as securities sales advertising to ensure they do not violate standards or regulations; advise technical staff on the development or use of environmental compliance or reporting tools; conduct environmental audits to ensure compliance with environmental standards; evaluate test procedures to conform to environmental monitoring program specifications; review or modify policies or operating guidelines to comply with changes in environmental standards or regulations; and direct environmental programs such as air or water compliance, aboveground or underground storage tanks, spill prevention or control, hazardous waste or materials management, solid waste recycling, medical waste management, indoor air quality, integrated pest management, employee training or disaster preparedness. The 29 tasks form a 20Core/9Supplemental occupational task pool; no single position is required to do all of them. Specialized tasks such as securities advertising, environmental tools/audits/monitoring/programs and risk strategy are chosen according to the actual business; investigations, disciplinary handling, external reporting and disclosure each require verifying the real jurisdiction, duties and authorization.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether compliance risk identification and prioritization have a verifiable basis; whether policies and procedures are documented and implemented and communicated; whether internal review and monitoring are sufficient to find real problems; whether the evidence gathering and interviews and conclusions of internal investigations are compliant and reviewable; whether external reporting and whistleblower protection and confidentiality are carried out as legally required; and whether remediation and training form a closed and traceable loop.
Check one: do compliance risk identification and prioritization have a verifiable basis

Assess risks and set priorities based on regulatory requirements, business and product risk, historical incidents and complaint data; document the assessment method and conclusions, and do not arbitrarily lower the level of an already identified risk because of business pressure.
Check two: are policies and procedures documented and implemented and communicated

Verify that regulatory policies and procedures have been documented, implemented and communicated; after a policy update, revise the training and checklists in step and retain the version and effective date; do not equate "issued" with "implemented."
Check three: are internal review and monitoring sufficient to find real problems

Conduct periodic internal reviews or audits covering high-risk areas; state the review scope and method and sampling and conclusions clearly; when deviations are found, record and escalate per procedure, and do not substitute "we reminded them" for remediation tracking.
Check four: is the evidence gathering and interviewing and conclusion of internal investigations compliant and reviewable

Conduct investigations per employer procedures and applicable regulations, specifying the scope and evidence gathering and interviews and preservation methods; consult corporate attorneys per procedure on difficult legal questions; base conclusions on evidence and state the basis and uncertainty, without presupposing the conclusion.
Check five: are external reporting and whistleblower protection and confidentiality carried out as legally required

O*NET includes confidential contact and reporting tasks; protection, anti-retaliation and escalation measures are confirmed under the applicable regime. China's Measures for the Compliance Management of Central Enterprises apply to central enterprises for which SASAC performs the duties of an investor; the U.S. DOJ2024 compliance assessment is guidance for assessing individual criminal prosecution cases, not a uniform rule for all employers in every country. Investigation, reporting, confidentiality, protection and data authority are verified against the actual jurisdiction, industry and authorization.
Check six: do remediation and training form a closed and traceable loop

The editor recommends tracking the remediation basis, verification materials and training feedback; verify the scope, recipient, timing and authorization of management reports and external reports separately, and do not submit all remediation and training records to regulators as a matter of course.

paragraphs: The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: understanding of regulations and rules, record and documentation ability, and awareness of review and communication and cross-department collaboration. The real difference lies in the scope of duties and the counterpart: chief executives are accountable for the organization's overall results; administrative services managers coordinate administration and logistics; security managers are responsible for the safety of people and assets and premises; regulatory affairs managers focus on regulatory registration and filing; compliance officers carry out transactional execution and support; environmental compliance inspectors focus on inspection and monitoring under environmental regulations; and this occupation is responsible within the organization for the planning and direction of compliance programs, internal review and investigation, and external compliance reporting and a closed remediation loop. When choosing, it is advisable to first validate with one deliverable exercise in "risk identification — policy and training points — review and investigation report points," rather than comparing titles first.

The comparison is based on the O*NET occupational definition, tasks, activities, context and public materials on adjacent occupations; it distinguishes by organizational duties, outputs and actual authority, and is an editorial compilation.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: chief executives, administrative services managers, security managers, regulatory affairs managers, compliance officers and environmental compliance inspectors. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what the direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Chief executives are responsible for overall organizational strategy and business results and external relations, and compliance is only one of their topics; this occupation is responsible for program planning and review and investigation and reporting within the compliance specialty.
People willing to be accountable for the results of the whole organization suit that direction; people willing to go deep in the compliance specialty suit this occupation.
Mainly strategy and business results and external commitments.
Chief executives

Administrative services managers coordinate support functions such as administration and logistics and facilities and procurement; this occupation focuses on adherence to compliance standards and review and investigation and reporting.
People willing to coordinate administration and logistics and procurement suit that direction; people willing to focus on the compliance specialty suit this occupation.
Mainly administration and facilities and procurement and budget execution.
Administrative services managers

Security managers are responsible for safety and security management and emergency plans for people and assets and premises; this occupation is responsible for adherence to compliance standards and investigation and reporting; the two interface on incident handling but have different objectives.
People willing to coordinate safety and security and emergency response suit that direction; people willing to do rule adherence and investigation and reporting suit this occupation.
Mainly safety and security and emergency plan records.
Security managers

Regulatory affairs managers center on product registration and regulatory filing and communication, submitting materials to regulators; this occupation centers on compliance adherence within the organization, and review and investigation and internal reporting.
People willing to do product registration and regulatory filing suit that direction; people willing to do compliance programs and investigations inside the organization suit this occupation.
Mainly registration and filing and regulatory communication records.
Regulatory affairs managers

Compliance officers carry out the transactional work of compliance policy execution and review and investigation; this occupation carries the responsibility for planning and directing organization-level compliance programs and for external reporting.
People willing to execute compliance tasks and support investigations suit that direction; people willing to be accountable for compliance programs and reporting suit this occupation.
Mainly compliance transactional execution and review and investigation records.
Compliance officers

Environmental compliance inspectors mainly inspect, monitor and test under environmental regulations, usually working at specific sites; this occupation centers on the planning and direction of compliance programs inside the organization and on investigation and reporting.
People willing to do environmental inspection and monitoring suit that direction; people willing to do compliance programs and investigations inside the organization suit this occupation.
Mainly environmental inspection and monitoring and testing records.

Direct answer: the risks this occupation most needs to judge in advance come from three places — reporting, whistleblowing and confidentiality obligations not being properly fulfilled; the evidence gathering and interviewing and conclusion procedures of internal investigations being non-compliant; and compliance programs and monitoring being insufficient to find real problems; conflict with business departments and impaired independence, training and policies not being implemented, and remediation not closing the loop will amplify these three types of risk.

The remaining risk scenarios are editorial suggestions.
Positions responsible for reporting and confidentiality and whistleblower channels

Failure to carry out applicable reporting or protection requirements creates legal, trust and incident-handling risk; the specific obligations and consequences depend on the jurisdiction and the facts, and no universal statutory deadline is set.

The editor recommends establishing controlled reporting channels, minimum necessary identity access and anti-retaliation handling; the central-enterprise measures and the DOJ assessment each provide a governance basis within their scope, and actual disclosure is verified by legal and authorized positions.

Delaying reporting on the grounds of "fear of hurting the business"; discussing identifiable whistleblower information in uncontrolled channels; passing whistleblower content to the reported party to handle itself.
Positions responsible for internal review and investigation

Missing procedural or evidentiary items may weaken the reviewability of investigation conclusions, disciplinary handling and reporting; the specific legal effect is judged by the rules and the facts, and it is not guaranteed that conclusions will necessarily be overturned.

Editor's control suggestions: conduct investigations per employer procedures and applicable regulations, specifying the scope and evidence gathering and interviews and evidence preservation methods; consult corporate attorneys per procedure on difficult legal questions; base conclusions on evidence and state the basis and uncertainty. The specific measures are verified under the applicable regime and are not a uniform statutory process for all organizations in every country.
Presupposing a position and gathering evidence selectively; substituting hearsay for verifiable evidence; leaving no documentation of interviews and evidence preservation.
Positions responsible for compliance programs and monitoring

Gaps in monitoring coverage may delay the discovery of problems; regulatory or reputational consequences require actual facts and applicable rules, and no guarantee of simultaneous occurrence is given. The DOJ assessment also makes clear that the occurrence of a violation does not by itself prove that a compliance program is ineffective.

Editor's control suggestions: determine the priority and frequency of review and monitoring based on risk assessment, covering high-risk areas; state the review scope and method and sampling and conclusions clearly; when deviations are found, record and escalate per procedure and track remediation. The specific measures are verified under the applicable regime and are not a uniform statutory process for all organizations in every country.
Doing only routine checks in low-risk areas; substituting "we reminded them" for remediation tracking; using past inspection results in place of the current assessment.
Positions responsible for implementing policy and training

Failure to implement policy and training may affect employee understanding and execution; whether there is a violation and whether obligations have been fulfilled require actual rules and facts, and issuance of a document or attendance sign-in does not directly prove effectiveness.

Editor's control suggestions: verify that policies and procedures have been documented, implemented and communicated; ensure training reaches the position and retain attendance and assessment records; after a policy update, revise the training and checklists in step and retain the version. The specific measures are verified under the applicable regime and are not a uniform statutory process for all organizations in every country.
Equating issuing a document with implementation; substituting a single all-staff email for necessary training; not updating the training and checklists after a policy update.
Positions responsible for independence and cross-departmental drive

Business pressure and insufficient autonomous resources may hinder identification and reporting; the specific risk is verified against the organizational structure and records, and a systematic underestimation is not asserted as inevitable.

The editor recommends confirming the independent reporting line and the escalation path for major risks under the actual regime; the central-enterprise measures set out the organizational duties of the enterprises they apply to, and the DOJ assesses autonomous resources according to enterprise size and risk, without requiring the same organization chart for all employers.
Assessing compliance staff against business indicators; reporting major risks only to business heads; not approving exceptions in writing.

Missing remediation or records items may make the causes and measures hard to review, and do not prove that problems will necessarily recur or that action has been taken; actual verification materials are needed.

Remediation should list the responsible persons, verification materials and closure criteria; report to management per policy, and whether and when to report to regulators is determined by the actually applicable rules.

Editorial summaries (capability stages, risk scenarios, exercise materials and the seven-day schedule) are stated separately from source facts, and their nature is marked in the corresponding places: the three work areas and six duties come from the official definition and task list, while the capability stages and risk scenarios and exercises are all editorial compilations, among which the exercise materials are entirely fictitious and must not be used for real compliance and investigation and reporting decisions or as a legal basis.

The two figures shown in the mainland China section are statistical aggregate and position-category average wage proxies (106,080 yuan/year for employees of enterprises above the designated size; 210,016 yuan/year for middle-level and above managers in enterprises above the designated size), not this occupation's median, starting pay or monthly pay, and this page does not use them to derive an occupation-level figure; the O*NET page for this occupation provides neither a separate wage and employment figure for 11-9199.02 nor industry or regional median wages, and this page has registered the corresponding gaps; statements involving reporting and investigation and protection and data are general frameworks and do not replace the text of the applicable regulations or legal advice.

paragraphs: This round verified the nine modules section by section and against their sources; correct current tasks and the wage projection are retained, jurisdictional and parent-occupation coverage is added, and shared facts are isolated. For local author self-review only.

O*NET current occupational and hiring data, OEWS2025 parent occupation wages, the BLS2025—2035 parent occupation projection, NBS2025 publication; the ILO2025 public research page, the NIST1.0 voluntary framework, and the central-enterprise measures / DOJ2024 related texts are used within their respective scopes.
Retrieval and nine-module revision for this round: 2026-10-09.

Precise occupational wages and national recruitment mapping for China, U.S. sub-class and industry wages, AI reliability adoption effects, personality validity, and certification fee conditions are still missing; old fact sources outside the shared scope are retained and reported, and no full-page or formal acceptance was performed.

subject.name: Compliance Managers
subject.summary: Compliance managers plan, direct or coordinate organizational activities so that they comply with ethical or regulatory standards; the work includes policy training, risk monitoring, internal review and investigation, documentation and reporting, coordination with attorneys and auditors, and specialized compliance carried out according to the position. Investigations and external reporting are carried out by actually authorized positions under the applicable rules.
